evidence.claim: Utah’s legislature designated its Utah length the Bluff to Monument Valley Scenic Byway; it also forms part of the Trail of the Ancients National Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: The length of US 163 in Utah has been designated the Bluff to Monument Valley Scenic Byway by the Utah State Legislature and forms part of the Trail of the Ancients National Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: Utah’s Canyon Country highlights the desert formations and river crossing and allows two hours for the drive.
evidence.quote: Allow 2 hours for the drive

evidence.claim: The Utah route first received the State Route 47 designation in 1910.
evidence.quote: The modern routing of US 163 in Utah was initially designated as State Route 47, in 1910.

evidence.claim: In 1970, a rearrangement of Four Corners highways made it part of US 163, which then extended north to Crescent Junction.
evidence.quote: In 1970, US 163 was designated along SR 464 in Arizona and SR 47 in Utah as part of a re-alignment of U.S. highways in the Four Corners region. With the re-alignment, US 160 was re-routed into Arizona instead of Utah. US 163 also absorbed the former route of US 160 to its former terminus at Interstate 70 at Crescent Junction.

evidence.claim: US 191 took over much of that northern alignment in 1981, and Utah shortened US 163 to Bluff.
evidence.quote: In 1981, AASHTO approved a new iteration of U.S. Route 191 that absorbed much of the alignment of US 163. Utah truncated US 163 at Bluff.

evidence.claim: From the Arizona line, the drive passes the junction for the Monument Valley visitor center and heads northeast to Mexican Hat.
evidence.quote: Just after it enters Utah, the highway junctions with the Monument Valley Visitors center. The highway proceeds northeast until the town of Mexican Hat

evidence.claim: There it crosses the San Juan and leaves the Navajo Nation.
evidence.quote: where the highway both crosses the San Juan River and exits the Navajo Nation.

evidence.claim: Beyond Mexican Hat, the route turns east across Comb Ridge toward Bluff.
evidence.quote: From Mexican Hat, the highway travels east crossing the Comb Ridge toward its terminus in Bluff.

evidence.claim: A view area near Utah mile marker 13 acquired the nickname Forrest Gump hill from the film location where the title character ends his cross-country run.
evidence.quote: a specific view area near Utah mile marker 13 has recently been given the nickname Forrest Gump hill, as a location from the movie Forrest Gump. It has become common for fans of the film to re-create the scene where the title character ends a cross country jogging along this point on US 163.

evidence.claim: The film’s wider frame includes Eagle Mesa, Brighams Tomb and Stagecoach.
evidence.quote: the mesa appears to the right of the frame in the widescreen version of the film, along with Brighams Tomb and Stagecoach.

evidence.claim: Eagle Mesa is visible from Highway 163 on Navajo Nation land.
evidence.quote: Eagle Mesa is situated 4.5 miles (7.2 km) northeast of Oljato–Monument Valley, Utah, on Navajo Nation land. It is, together with Setting Hen, an iconic landform of Monument Valley and can be seen from Highway 163.

evidence.claim: Its cliffs rise above Organ Rock Shale, which erodes more readily than the sandstone above it.
evidence.quote: The bottom layer is Organ Rock Shale, the next stratum is cliff-forming De Chelly Sandstone

evidence.claim: That unequal erosion helped shape the valley’s mesas and buttes.
evidence.quote: The buttes and mesas of Monument Valley are the result of the Organ Rock Shale being more easily eroded than the overlaying sandstone.

evidence.claim: Mexican Hat takes its name from the sombrero-shaped rock on the northeast edge of town, a formation 60 feet wide and 12 feet high.
evidence.quote: The name "Mexican Hat" comes from a curiously sombrero-shaped rock outcropping on the northeast edge of town; the rock measures 60-foot (18 m) wide by 12-foot (3.7 m).

evidence.claim: The settlement stands on the San Juan River at the northern edge of the Navajo Nation.
evidence.quote: It is on the San Juan River on the northern edge of the Navajo Nation's borders

evidence.claim: In 2016, the US 163 river crossing received the name Jason R. Workman Memorial Bridge.
evidence.quote: In 2016, the U.S. Route 163 bridge crossing the San Juan River on the southern border of the town was renamed the "Jason R. Workman Memorial Bridge",

evidence.claim: Workman, a 1997 graduate of nearby San Juan High School, served with SEAL Team Six and was killed in Afghanistan in 2011.
evidence.quote: after a member of SEAL Team Six who was killed in action in Afghanistan on August 6, 2011. Workman was a 1997 graduate of the nearby San Juan High School.

evidence.claim: Bluff’s name comes from the bluffs near its town site.
evidence.quote: The town was named for the bluffs near the town site.

evidence.claim: Under John Taylor’s direction, Silas S. Smith and Jens Nielson led about 230 Mormons toward southeastern Utah to establish a farming community.
evidence.quote: Under the direction of John Taylor, Silas S. Smith and Danish settler Jens Nielson led about 230 Mormons on an expedition to start a farming community in southeastern Utah.

evidence.claim: They arrived in April 1880 after forging about 200 miles of trail over difficult terrain, including the passage down Hole in the Rock.
evidence.quote: After forging about 200 miles (320 kilometers) of their own trail over difficult terrain, the settlers arrived on the site of Bluff in April 1880. (The trail followed went over and down the "Hole in the Rock",

evidence.claim: The town lies where Cottonwood Wash meets the San Juan, on the north margin of the river valley.
evidence.quote: The community is on the north margin of the San Juan River valley at the confluence of Cottonwood Wash with the San Juan.

evidence.claim: The road signs and the national designation did not immediately agree: the northern section remained unsigned, and federal approval to end US 163 at US 191 came in 2008.
evidence.quote: Although the state changed the definition of US 163 back to match the national definition in 2004, the portion north of Bluff remained unsigned. In October 2008, UDOT requested and obtained approval to truncate US 163 to the junction with US 191 resolving the discrepancy.

evidence.claim: Bluff sits at the meeting of Cottonwood Wash and the San Juan River.
evidence.quote: The community is on the north margin of the San Juan River valley at the confluence of Cottonwood Wash with the San Juan.

evidence.claim: Eagle Mesa rises 1,100 feet above its surroundings; its upper rock layers include the Moenkopi Formation capped by Shinarump Conglomerate.
evidence.quote: the summit rises 1,100 feet (335 meters) above surrounding terrain

evidence.claim: its upper rock layers include the Moenkopi Formation capped by Shinarump Conglomerate.
evidence.quote: the upper layer is Moenkopi Formation capped by Shinarump Conglomerate.

evidence.claim: Beyond the crossing, Valley of the Gods lies to the north on US 163, with Goosenecks State Park west-northwest of town.
evidence.quote: Goosenecks State Park is located 9 miles (14 km) west-northwest,  Alhambra Rock is 6 miles (10 km) west-southwest, and the Valley of the Gods is to the north on U.S. 163.

evidence.claim: Its population fell to seventy by 1930, then rose during the uranium prospecting boom of the 1950s before declining again with uranium in the 1970s.
evidence.quote: The town's population had declined to seventy by 1930 but rebounded during a uranium prospecting boom in the 1950s. With the uranium decline in the 1970s, Bluff again declined
